chapters.name: Chapter 1: Act fast and keep a heart going

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Check, call, care: the first minute
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check the scene and the person, then call 911 with a clear message.
This lesson builds toward: Given an emergency scene described in words, you will check the scene for danger, check whether the person responds, and call 911 or the local emergency number, in the right order, saying the address and what happened in one clear sentence.
In any emergency, start with three words: check, call, care. First CHECK that the scene is safe for you: traffic, fire, smoke, electricity, an angry person or deep water. If it is not safe, stay back and call. You cannot help anyone if you get hurt too.
Then check the person. Tap their shoulder and shout, "Are you okay?" Look at their chest for normal breathing. Gasping now and then is NOT normal breathing.
Next CALL 911 (or your local emergency number outside the US). If someone is with you, point at them and say, "You, call 911 and bring an AED." Put the phone on speaker. Say the address first, then what happened, and do not hang up until the dispatcher tells you to. The dispatcher can coach you through CPR.
Then CARE: give the help you can until trained help arrives. Use gloves or a barrier if you have them. Many US states have Good Samaritan laws that protect people who help in good faith; the details differ by state.
Step by step:
- Check the scene: is it safe for me?
- Check the person: tap, shout "Are you okay?", look for normal breathing.
- Call 911 (or your local number), or point at one person to call and another to bring an AED.
- Phone on speaker: address first, then what happened. Stay on the line.
- Care: help until trained help arrives.
Words to know:
- Dispatcher: the trained person who answers 911 calls, sends help and can tell you what to do.
- Unresponsive: a person who does not move, open their eyes or answer when you tap and shout.
- Good Samaritan law: a state law that protects people who help in an emergency in good faith; the details differ by state.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus (US National Library of Medicine): CPR - adult and child after onset of puberty
- American Red Cross: First Aid, CPR and AED classes
Try it now: Write the one sentence you would say to 911 from your home: your full address with the nearest cross street, then "a man collapsed and is not breathing". Read it out loud twice until you can say it without looking.
You can now check the scene and the person, and call 911 with a clear message.

check.q: You see a man lying in the road and cars are passing. What do you do first?
options: Make sure the scene is safe for you, then call 911
check.why: Checking that the scene is safe comes first; if it is not safe, stay back and call.

check.q: On the call to 911, what do you say first?
check.why: The address comes first so help can be sent even if the call drops.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Hands-Only CPR: push hard and fast
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the steps of Hands-Only CPR in the right order.
This lesson builds toward: Given an adult who collapses and is not breathing normally, you will list the steps of Hands-Only CPR and of using an AED, in the right order, with hand position, a rate of 100 to 120 a minute and a depth of about 2 inches.
When an adult suddenly collapses, is unresponsive and is not breathing normally, the heart may have stopped. This is called cardiac arrest. CPR pushes blood to the brain until an AED and emergency crews arrive.
The American Heart Association teaches Hands-Only CPR for anyone not trained or not confident giving breaths: call 911, then push hard and fast in the center of the chest. You do not need to check for a pulse unless you are a health professional.
Kneel beside the person on a firm, flat surface. Put the heel of one hand in the center of the chest, the other hand on top, arms straight, shoulders over your hands. Press down about 2 inches (5 centimeters), at 100 to 120 pushes a minute, and let the chest come all the way back up each time.
Keep going until an AED is ready, trained help takes over, or the person starts to breathe normally. CPR is tiring: if someone else knows how, switch about every two minutes with little pause. A class lets you practice the depth on a manikin; never practice on a real person.
Step by step:
- Unresponsive and not breathing normally: call 911 and send for an AED.
- Lay the person on their back on a firm, flat surface.
- Heel of one hand in the center of the chest, other hand on top.
- Arms straight, shoulders over hands.
- Push about 2 inches deep, 100 to 120 times a minute; let the chest rise all the way.
- Do not stop until an AED, trained help, or normal breathing.
Words to know:
- CPR: cardiopulmonary resuscitation: chest compressions (and sometimes rescue breaths) that keep blood moving when the heart stops.
- Cardiac arrest: when the heart suddenly stops pumping; the person collapses and does not breathe normally.
- Compression: one push down on the chest.
- Manikin: a practice body used in CPR classes.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus (US National Library of Medicine): CPR - adult and child after onset of puberty
- American Heart Association: CPR and First Aid courses
Try it now: Kneel by a firm pillow or a rolled towel on the floor (never a person). Place your hands as shown, arms straight. Set a phone timer for 30 seconds and count your pushes out loud. Aim for 50 to 60 pushes in 30 seconds, which matches 100 to 120 a minute.
You can now list the steps of Hands-Only CPR and keep the right rate.

check.q: Where do your hands go for adult CPR?
options: In the center of the chest
check.why: The heel of one hand goes in the center of the chest with the other hand on top.

check.q: How fast do you push in CPR?
check.why: Guidance is 100 to 120 compressions a minute, letting the chest rise each time.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Using an AED, and what a full CPR class adds
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the steps of using an AED with CPR.
This lesson builds toward: Given an adult who collapses and is not breathing normally, you will list the steps of Hands-Only CPR and of using an AED, in the right order, with hand position, a rate of 100 to 120 a minute and a depth of about 2 inches.
An AED (automated external defibrillator) is a small box that can shock a heart back into a normal rhythm. You find them in schools, gyms, airports, offices, malls and places of worship, often in a wall case with a heart and lightning sign.
AEDs are made for people with no training. Turn it on and it talks to you. Bare the chest, wipe it dry, put the pads where the pictures show, and plug in the cable if needed. Everyone stands clear while it checks the heart. If it says to shock, make sure no one is touching the person and press the button. Then go straight back to CPR, as the AED tells you.
Use the AED as soon as it arrives, and follow its voice exactly. Do not stop CPR to go and look for one yourself if someone else can bring it.
In a full CPR class you also learn rescue breaths: 30 compressions, then 2 breaths, repeated. You also learn CPR for children and babies, which is different. Practice those steps in class with an instructor.
Step by step:
- Keep CPR going while someone brings the AED.
- Turn the AED on and listen.
- Bare and dry the chest; put the pads where the pictures show.
- Stand clear while it checks; no one touches the person.
- If it says shock: everyone clear, press the button.
- Go straight back to CPR as it tells you.
Words to know:
- AED: automated external defibrillator: a box that checks the heart and, if needed, gives a shock to reset its rhythm. It talks you through each step.
- Pads: sticky patches with wires that go on the bare chest so the AED can check the heart and shock it.
- Rescue breaths: breaths you give into the person's mouth during CPR; learned in a full class.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus (US National Library of Medicine): CPR - adult and child after onset of puberty
- American Heart Association: CPR and First Aid courses
- American Red Cross: First Aid, CPR and AED classes
Try it now: Find out where the nearest AED is at your work, school, gym or place of worship. Ask a manager or look for the sign. Write down exactly where it is, and draw the two pad places on a stick figure from memory.
You can now list the steps of using an AED with CPR and say where the nearest one is.

check.q: The AED says a shock is advised. What do you do before you press the button?
options: Make sure no one is touching the person
check.why: Everyone must be clear so the shock goes only to the person.

check.q: The AED has given a shock. What next?
options: Go back to CPR as the AED tells you
check.why: After a shock you go straight back to CPR, following the AED's voice.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Common emergencies and getting certified

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Choking and severe bleeding
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Identify choking, and describe how to stop severe bleeding with direct pressure.
This lesson builds toward: Given a description of an adult who may be choking, you will identify the signs of choking and describe the first aid, telling apart a person who can cough and talk from one who cannot. Given a wound that is bleeding heavily, you will describe how to control the bleeding with firm, direct pressure, naming gloves or a barrier, pressure that does not stop, and adding layers instead of lifting the cloth.
Choking: a person may grab their throat, be unable to talk, cough weakly, make a high-pitched sound or turn bluish. Ask, "Are you choking? Can you speak?" If they can cough hard and talk, do not hit them; tell them to keep coughing.
If they cannot speak, cough or breathe, have someone call 911. US guidance shows two ways to push the object out: firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand (back blows), and quick inward-and-upward pushes just above the belly button (abdominal thrusts). Pregnant or very large people get chest thrusts instead. If the person passes out, call 911, lower them to the floor and start CPR. Learn and practice these moves in class; do not practice thrusts on a real person.
Severe bleeding: call 911. Put on gloves if you have them, or use a plastic bag as a barrier. Press hard, right on the wound, with a clean cloth, gauze or even a piece of clothing, and keep pressing. Do not lift it to look. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top and keep pressing.
Do not pull out an object stuck in a wound; pad around it. A tourniquet is for life-threatening bleeding on an arm or leg when pressure is not enough; Stop the Bleed and first aid classes teach how to use one.
Step by step:
- Choking: ask "Are you choking? Can you speak?"
- Can cough and talk: let them keep coughing.
- Cannot speak or breathe: call 911 and give the first aid you learned in class (back blows and abdominal thrusts).
- Passes out: lower to the floor, start CPR.
- Bleeding: call 911, gloves or a barrier, press hard on the wound with a clean cloth.
- Soaks through: add layers on top; do not lift the first cloth.
Words to know:
- Abdominal thrusts: quick inward and upward pushes just above the belly button to force out a blockage; sometimes called the Heimlich maneuver.
- Back blows: firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand to loosen a blockage.
- Direct pressure: pressing firmly right on a wound to slow and stop bleeding.
- Tourniquet: a tight band put on an arm or leg above a wound to stop life-threatening bleeding; taught in class.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Choking - adult or child over 1 year
- MedlinePlus: Bleeding
- American Red Cross: First Aid, CPR and AED classes
Try it now: Put a folded towel on your own forearm. Press down hard with the flat of your hand for 60 seconds by the clock without lifting. Then add a second towel on top and keep pressing. Write two lines: how hard it was to keep pressure, and the three choking signs from this lesson.
You can now spot the signs of choking and stop severe bleeding with firm, direct pressure.

check.q: A woman at lunch is coughing hard and can still talk. What do you do?
options: Hit her back hard right away
Encourage her to keep coughing and stay with her
check.why: If a person can cough hard and talk, let them keep coughing; do not hit them.

check.q: Blood soaks through the cloth you are pressing on a wound. What do you do?
options: Put more cloth on top and keep pressing
check.why: Adding layers keeps pressure on; lifting the cloth can start the bleeding again.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Spotting a heart attack and a stroke
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Recognize the warning signs of a heart attack and a stroke.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of symptoms, you will recognize the warning signs of a heart attack and of a stroke using B.E. F.A.S.T., getting at least 4 of 5 right and calling 911 instead of driving the person.
A heart attack is when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked. Common signs: chest pain or pressure that may spread to the jaw, arm, back or stomach, shortness of breath, cold sweat, feeling sick or dizzy, and unusual tiredness. Women, older adults and people with diabetes may have milder or different signs.
If you think it is a heart attack, call 911 right away. Do not wait to see if it passes, and do not let the person talk you out of it. Have them sit and rest, loosen tight clothes, and stay with them. Give no medicine unless it is their own prescribed medicine or the 911 dispatcher tells you to. If they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED.
A stroke is when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a blood vessel bursts. The CDC teaches B.E. F.A.S.T.: Balance (sudden dizziness or loss of balance), Eyes (sudden trouble seeing), Face (ask them to smile; does one side droop?), Arms (ask them to raise both arms; does one drift down?), Speech (is it slurred or strange?), Time (call 911 right away).
Note the time the signs started and tell the crew. Call an ambulance; do not drive the person to the hospital yourself.
Step by step:
- Heart attack signs: chest pain or pressure, short of breath, cold sweat, sick, dizzy.
- Call 911 right away; sit them down, loosen clothes, stay with them.
- No medicine unless it is theirs or the dispatcher says so.
- Stroke: check B.E. F.A.S.T.
- Note the time the signs started; call an ambulance, do not drive them.
Words to know:
- Heart attack: when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked; the person is usually awake and has chest pain or pressure.
- Stroke: when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a blood vessel in the brain bursts.
- B.E. F.A.S.T.: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech, Time: a way to spot a stroke and remember to call 911.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Heart attack first aid
- CDC: Signs and Symptoms of Stroke
Try it now: Write B.E. F.A.S.T. down the side of a page. Next to each letter, write the question or test you would use, from memory. Then teach it to one friend or family member in under one minute.
You can now recognize the warning signs of a heart attack and a stroke and call 911 fast.

check.q: Your uncle's smile droops on one side and his words are slurred. What do you do?
options: Call 911 right away and note the time
Let him lie down and sleep it off
Drive him to the hospital yourself
check.why: These are stroke signs; call 911 at once, note the time, and let the ambulance take him.

check.q: Which is a common sign of a heart attack?
options: A small cut on the hand
Chest pain or pressure that spreads to the arm or jaw
An itchy rash on the leg
check.why: Chest pain or pressure that may spread is a common heart attack sign.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Getting certified: your readiness plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose an in-person CPR and first aid class and write a training plan with a date.
This lesson builds toward: Using the American Red Cross or American Heart Association class finder, you will choose an in-person CPR, AED and first aid class and write a training plan with a date, naming the course, who grants the certificate and whether your job needs it.
This course gives awareness, not a certificate. Employers who ask for CPR and first aid usually want a card from a recognized provider. In the US the best known are the American Red Cross and the American Heart Association. Both have class finders on their websites.
Pick the right class for your path. Many workplace and community jobs (child care, coaching, security, food service, nonprofits) accept an adult and pediatric First Aid, CPR and AED class. Healthcare jobs (nurse aide, EMT, pharmacy and medical students) usually need Basic Life Support (BLS). Ask your employer or program which one they accept before you pay.
Many classes are blended: part online, then an in-person skills session with an instructor and manikins. A fully online class with no hands-on test may not be accepted. Prices, class length and how long the card lasts differ: check the provider's page and the date on your card, and renew before it runs out.
Ask about free or low-cost classes: some employers, workforce programs, fire departments, hospitals and community groups offer them. OSHA says employers must have first aid people and supplies that fit the hazards of the workplace.
Step by step:
- Ask your employer or program which class they accept (for example First Aid, CPR and AED, or BLS).
- Open the Red Cross or American Heart Association class finder.
- Choose an in-person or blended class near you.
- Write the course name, who grants the card, place, date and cost.
- Put the date in your calendar and set a reminder before the card expires.
Words to know:
- Certification card: proof from the training provider that you passed the skills test; employers ask to see it.
- BLS: Basic Life Support: the CPR class for healthcare workers and students.
- Blended learning: a class that is part online and part in person, with a hands-on skills test.
- Pediatric: for children and babies.
Official sources:
- American Red Cross: First Aid, CPR and AED classes
- American Heart Association: CPR and First Aid courses
- OSHA: Medical and First Aid
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page First Aid and CPR Readiness Plan. Write your emergency number and address sentence, where the nearest AED and first aid kit are, the emergency steps from memory, and an in-person class you found on the Red Cross or AHA site: name, who grants it, place and date.
You can now choose a recognized in-person CPR and first aid class and plan when you will take it.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Emergency call ready No emergency number or address sentence, or the address is unclear. Has the right emergency number and a clear sentence with the address first, then what happened. Also adds a cross street or landmark and practices saying it out loud. AED and kit located Does not know where an AED or first aid kit is. Names where the nearest AED and first aid kit are at home, work, school or place of worship. Names two places, and checked that the AED case is reachable. Steps in order Steps are missing or in the wrong order, or CPR rate and depth are wrong. Writes check, call, CPR and AED in order, with center-of-chest hands, 100 to 120 a minute and about 2 inches. Also writes the AED steps and when to switch rescuers. Choking and bleeding Mixes up what to do, or says to lift the cloth or pull out an object. Writes the choking signs (O3) and firm, direct pressure with layers for bleeding. Also says when a choking person needs CPR and what a tourniquet is for. Heart attack and stroke Cannot list B.E. F.A.S.T. or heart attack signs. Lists B.E. F.A.S.T. and three heart attack signs, with "call 911". Also notes to record the time signs started and not to drive the person. Certification plan No class chosen, or an online-only class with no skills test. Names an in-person or blended class, who grants the card, the place and a date. Also confirmed with the employer or program that the class is accepted, and set a renewal reminder. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: You finished this awareness course. What does it give you?
options: A CPR card your employer must accept
Knowledge to prepare you for an in-person certification class
check.why: This course prepares you; the certificate comes from an in-person class with a recognized provider.

check.q: You are starting a nurse aide program. Which CPR class do they most likely want?
options: A fully online video with no skills test
A class from a social media post
Basic Life Support (BLS), after checking with the program
check.why: Healthcare programs usually require BLS; ask the program to confirm which one they accept.
